title: Behavioral Reset for Elevated Sleep Latency
description: Time-to-fall-asleep has moved meaningfully above your personal baseline for at least one night — a signal of elevated pre-sleep arousal (caffeine still active, late bright/blue light exposure, irregular bedtime) rather than a sleep disorder. Recommends behavioral adjustments first, not supplements.
source: Huberman Lab (caffeine timing, light exposure, sleep regularity); product heuristic (trigger threshold)

conditional.question: Did it take longer than usual to fall asleep last night?
conditional.yesLabel: Yes, help me adjust my evening routine

actions.action: Push caffeine intake earlier and add a firm cutoff
actions.timing: Delay first caffeine 90-120 minutes after waking; no caffeine within 8-10 hours of your target bedtime
actions.details: Caffeine has a long half-life and can extend sleep latency even when a person does not subjectively feel 'wired.' Delaying the first dose and setting a cutoff time are Huberman Lab's standard first-line adjustments before considering anything else.

Dim overhead lights and reduce screen brightness (or use night-mode/warm-light settings) in the 1-2 hours before bed. Bright, especially blue-enriched, light in the evening suppresses melatonin onset and delays the body's sleep-readiness signal.

actions.action: Anchor a consistent bed and wake time
actions.details: Keep bed and wake times within about a 30-minute window daily. Irregular sleep timing desynchronizes the circadian drive for sleep, which can independently lengthen how long it takes to fall asleep even when total sleep opportunity is adequate.

benefits: Addresses the most common behavioral drivers of elevated sleep latency before assuming anything is medically wrong
No supplements or medication involved — lowest-risk first response
Builds sleep-onset consistency over time rather than treating a single bad night in isolation
science: Sleep latency (time to fall asleep) is a well-established, easily measured marker of pre-sleep physiological and cognitive arousal. Elevated caffeine load at bedtime, late bright/blue light exposure, and irregular sleep timing are among the most consistently documented behavioral contributors to prolonged sleep latency in the sleep science literature, and are the standard first-line targets before considering supplements or clinical evaluation.
contraindications: Not a diagnosis or treatment for insomnia or another sleep disorder

If elevated sleep latency persists most nights over several weeks despite consistent behavioral changes, consider discussing with a physician or sleep specialist rather than continuing to self-manage indefinitely

estimated_impact.sleep_onset: Moderate improvement (over days to weeks of consistent behavior change)

evidence_metadata.scientific_rationale: Single-signal (sleep_latency), above 130% of personal rolling baseline for one night. Sleep latency as a signal of pre-sleep arousal/circadian misalignment is well established in the sleep literature; the specific 130%-of-baseline cutoff used to fire this rule is not independently validated.

evidence_for_protocol.notes: Caffeine-timing, evening light reduction, and consistent sleep/wake timing are all directly and repeatedly recommended by Huberman Lab specifically as first-line, non-supplement responses to trouble falling asleep.

evidence_for_trigger.notes: The 130%-of-baseline threshold and 1-night persistence window are a product heuristic, not derived from a cited study. Sleep latency naturally has higher night-to-night variance than metrics like HRV, so this threshold may need tuning (likely upward, to reduce false positives) once real outcome data exists. Deliberately single-signal (no AND with another metric) because sleep latency alone is already a fairly specific, low-stakes-to-be-wrong-about trigger — the recommended actions are safe even if the trigger is noise.

expected_effect.short_term: Unlikely to change same night; the recommended actions target the following evening's sleep latency, not the night that triggered the rule.
expected_effect.long_term: Consistent caffeine-timing, light-hygiene, and schedule-regularity changes are associated with reduced average sleep latency over weeks, though this exact rule/threshold combination has not been outcome-tested in this app.
